newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk anti-Islamist coalition wins confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Turk anti-Islamist coalition wins confidence vote.

text.p: Turkey's new anti-Islamist government sealed its grip on power after a rowdy confidence vote on Saturday that mirrored the divisions tearing at the country at large.

Parliament voted 281 to 256, to approve a coalition under Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz -- designed to keep the big Islam-based Welfare Party at bay and end months of social and political tensions over the role of religion in public life.
But the session degenerated into mayhem as rival Islamist and secularist MPs exchanged heated insults and even a flurry of punches, forcing several delays in the balloting.
Witnesses said one Welfare deputy drew a pistol as the row spilled into the corridors. No shots were fired.
"A new era is beginning in Turkey," a determined Yilmaz told the parliament minutes after victory.
"The first step we will take is to return everything to normality. Our nation is sick of disputes," said Yilmaz, 50.
The final results confirmed a return to power for Turkey's secularists, after one year and one day under Welfare chief Necmettin Erbakan, the modern republic's first Islamist leader.
It also appeared to spell a realignment among Turkey's fractious political parties, particularly on the right where Yilmaz looks increasingly secure.
Eight deputies in the 550-member chamber, mostly dissidents from the rival conservative True Path Party of former prime minister Tansu Ciller, failed to appear for the vote.
Others True Path MPs openly defected to Yilmaz's Motherland Party, giving him a wider-than expected margin in the end.
Erbakan immediately condemned the new government and predicted its days were numbered.
"Turkey is facing the danger of moving step-by-step towards chaos and confusion," said Erbakan, who was effectively driven from power by the secularist establishment.

"This government does not have the staying power so it is obviously not going to get anywhere," he told a news conference after the vote. "Let's see how many days it will last. You'll notice I am talking about days."
Yilmaz's efforts to prevent a planned Islamist return to power were backed by President Suleyman Demirel and the army, which casts itself as defenders of the secularist order.

A Yilmaz aide said the generals had held back from steps to oust Erbakan when it became clear the secularist politicians could get rid of the Islamists on their own. Turkey's generals have deposed three civilian governments since 1960.

The anti-Islamist generals had openly criticised Erbakan, NATO member Turkey's first Islamist leader, for failing to heed army warnings to curb Moslem activism. The brass also turned on the secularist True Path for cooperating with Erbakan.
"An easy vote," predicted Milliyet daily. "The government...will win the parliamentary confidence ballot by at least 20 votes," the Yeni Yuzyil newspaper said.
In the event, Yilmaz and his conservative and leftist allies won by 25 votes.
On paper, the coalition partners command just 217 MPs in the 550-seat assembly. They must rely on the support of 49 other left-wing deputies and about 20 independents.
By contrast the main opposition Islamists field 157 deputies, while their conservative former allies in True Path have been reduced to no more than 98 seats.

In a fresh blow to True Path leader Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993 before handing over to Erbakan, three more deputies left the party shortly before the confidence vote.
She upset the secularists establishment by going into coalition with the Islamists last year and now faces the resurrection of old corruption allegations against her and her businessman husband.
Yilmaz has promised to introduce anti-Islamist legislation, particularly on education, and take Turkey closer to Europe.
But he has shown signs of backtracking on a promise of early elections next year, well before polls are due in the year 2000.
A key left-wing party warned it could withdraw its support for Yilmaz if he does not push elections legislation though parliament before a recess later this month.
